thag4.11:4.1: This is a difficult line. My reading depends on the speculative emending of the opening _tā_ to _te_. Then _matamada_ is “death-mad”, a fitting epithet for the snake who is the frogs’ predator. The commentary also identifies as snake, but reads _amatamada_, “intoxicated by the deathless”, further explaining _amata_ here as _agada_, “antidote”; but none of this strikes me as very likely. Norman (note 310 in *Elders Verses II*) notes Woodward’s suggested _sappahīnā_ (“rid of snakes”) for _suppahīnā_ (“well rid”) and further suggests “mad for the deathless” as a term for the _bhikkhus_. Norman takes this as a play on Sappaka’s name, but this requires that the river be “rid of Sappaka”, whereas the whole poem is about how he is content to stay there. Perhaps, “That Saṅgha mad for freedom from death is rid of snakes”, the idea being that the purity of the Saṅgha is like a charm that keeps the snakes away. This ends up substantially similar to my own suggestion, and chimes with the practice of the Saṅgha to recite chants dispelling snakes.
